Scone
SKOON
n. (the Perthshire Moot Hill where the kings of Scots were enthroned, and the Augustinian abbey burned in 1559)
Perhaps from Gaelic sgonn, a lump or mound, referring to the Moot Hill; the burgh spelling keeps the Scots pronunciation.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Scone, two miles above Perth on the Tay, is the place where the kings of Scots were made. The Moot Hill there held the Stone of Destiny until Edward I took it in 1296, and the enthronement at Scone, with the royal genealogy recited in Gaelic and the earls setting the king in the chair, was the act that made a king rather than a coronation by a bishop. Alexander I founded an Augustinian priory beside it about 1120, raised to an abbey, which kept the regalia and the records. In June 1559 the Reformation crowd from Perth came upstream and burned the abbey and the bishop's palace, against Knox's own attempts to restrain them. Charles II was crowned there in 1651, the last Scottish coronation. The dictionary records Scone for what an enthronement is and is not. A hill, a stone and a recited pedigree confer nothing; God is the judge who puts down one and sets up another, and the kingdom which is the LORD'S is not conveyed by any ceremony that men can perform or interrupt.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a throne as a royal seat; a judge as one who presides in a court or decides a question; to set up as to erect or establish; a governor as one who rules; and to pluck up as to tear out by the roots.

expand to see more

THRONE, n. A royal seat; a chair of state; the seat of a bishop; sovereign power and dignity.

JUDGE, n. A civil officer who is invested with authority to hear and determine causes; one who has skill to decide on any thing.

SET, v.t. To put or place; to fix; to establish; to appoint; to constitute, as to set up a king.

GOVERNOR, n. One who governs; one invested with supreme authority; a ruler; a director.

PLUCK, v.t. To pull with sudden force or effort; to pull off, out or up; to tear out by the roots.

Key Scripture

Psa 75:7 — "But God is the judge: he putteth down one, and setteth up another."

Dan 2:21 — "And he changeth the times and the seasons: he removeth kings, and setteth up kings: he giveth wisdom unto the wise, and knowledge to them that know understanding:"

Psa 22:28 — "For the kingdom is the LORD'S: and he is the governor among the nations."

Jer 18:7 — "At what instant I shall speak concerning a nation, and concerning a kingdom, to pluck up, and to pull down, and to destroy it;"

Modern Corruption

Perthshire Moot Hill where the kings of Scots were enthroned, with its Augustinian abbey, burned by the Reformation crowd in 1559.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that sovereignty is conferred by God and not by ceremony. The Psalmist sets the matter in a single line that leaves no office to the hill or the stone: “But God is the judge: he putteth down one, and setteth up another” (Psa 75:7). Daniel says the same of the greatest empires, “he removeth kings, and setteth up kings” (Dan 2:21), so that the recited pedigree at Scone described a providence it could not create.

The live temptation at a national shrine is to believe that the rite makes the thing, and then to fight over the rite. The Stone was carried to Westminster, carried back, and argued over for seven centuries; the abbey that kept it was burned by Protestants in a fortnight of rioting. Through all of it the title stood where Scripture puts it: “For the kingdom is the LORD'S: and he is the governor among the nations” (Psa 22:28). The same God reserves the right to undo any realm he has made, “to pluck up, and to pull down, and to destroy it” (Jer 18:7), which is a sobering word to read on a coronation hill.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew shaphat (H8199), to judge; Hebrew rum (H7311), to lift up; Hebrew mashal (H4910), to rule; Hebrew nathash (H5428), to pluck up.

expand to see more

Hebrew shaphat (H8199) — to judge, to govern; “But God is the judge”, Psalm 75:7.

Hebrew rum (H7311) — to be high, to lift up; the sense of “setteth up another”, Psalm 75:7.

Aramaic heada (H5709) — to remove, to pass on; “he removeth kings”, Daniel 2:21.

Hebrew mashal (H4910) — to rule, to have dominion; “he is the governor among the nations”, Psalm 22:28.

Hebrew nathash (H5428) — to pluck up, to root out; “to pluck up, and to pull down”, Jeremiah 18:7.

Usage

"“But God is the judge: he putteth down one, and setteth up another” (Psa 75:7) — what the Moot Hill did not do."

"“For the kingdom is the LORD'S” (Psa 22:28) — the title no stone conveys."

"“to pluck up, and to pull down, and to destroy it” (Jer 18:7) — read on a coronation hill."
